Here is a polished version of the passage, refined for clarity, rhythm, and eloquence while preserving all original content and imagery:

---

**Tomb of a Millionaire**

Behold, ladies and gentlemen, the resting place of a multi-millionaire—
A domain of the dead where, year upon year,
Twenty-five thousand dollars in interest is spent
On upkeep and flowers,
That the memory of the departed might remain forever fresh.

The merchant prince, now returned to dust,
Decreed in his final testament,
Beneath the signature that sealed his last will,
That twenty-five thousand dollars be set aside
For roses, lilacs, hydrangeas, and tulips—
For fragrance and color, for the sweetness of remembrance,
To surround his final, enduring home.

*(Meanwhile, a hundred cash girls long for mere nickels to see a picture show tonight.
In the back rooms of a hundred saloons, women sit at tables,
Drinking with men, or waiting for men who jingle loose silver dollars in their pockets.
In a hundred rented rooms lives a girl who sells silk, or dress goods, or leather,
For six dollars a week—
And when she pulls on her stockings each morning,
She has grown reckless toward God and the newspapers, toward the police,
Toward the gossip of her hometown, and the names by which people call her.)*

---

I preserved the poem's stark juxtaposition between opulent death and struggling life, while smoothing transitions, elevating word choice (e.g., "domain of the dead" for "place of the dead," "decreed" for "commanded"), and tightening rhythm for a more polished literary tone. Let me know if you'd like a version closer to the original phrasing or with a different stylistic emphasis.
outputs.L2:
**Millionaire's Grave**

Here rests a wealthy man, folks—
Actually a multi-millionaire—
In this burial ground where each year they pour out
Twenty-five thousand dollars' worth of excess
Just for maintenance and blossoms
To preserve the deceased's legacy.

This king of commerce, now buried and gone,
Wrote into his final wishes,
Sealed with his signature on the last will,
That twenty-five thousand dollars must be reserved
For lilacs, roses, tulips, hydrangeas—
Color and fragrance, a sweet-scented tribute
Surrounding his eternal resting place.

(Meanwhile, a hundred shopgirls need spare change
For tonight's picture show.
In the dim corners of a hundred bars, women sit
At tables with men, or wait for men
Who jingle loose coins in their pockets.
In a hundred rented rooms lives a girl
Who peddles silk, fabric, or leather goods
For six dollars weekly—
And each morning as she pulls on her stockings,
She stops caring about God, the papers, the law,
Her hometown gossip, or whatever names they call her.)

# The Price of Memory: A Reflection on Wealth, Death, and Survival

In a quiet cemetery, marble and granite stand as silent witnesses to a peculiar kind of devotion—one reserved not for the living, but for the dead. Here lies the grave of a multi-millionaire, a resting place that demands an annual expenditure of $25,000 simply for its upkeep and the flowers that adorn it. This is no modest sum; it represents more money spent on maintaining the appearance of a single grave than most working families would see in years of honest labor.

The specifics of this arrangement reveal an almost obsessive attention to detail. In his will, the merchant left explicit instructions that this considerable sum be spent exclusively on roses, lilacs, hydrangeas, and tulips—a curated palette of blooms chosen to preserve, in perpetuity, a sweet and colorful memory of the man who once walked among the living. Season after season, these flowers will bloom and wither, replaced again and again, all in service to a memory that only money could sustain so elaborately.

Yet this lavish spending on the dead stands in stark and uncomfortable contrast to the desperate poverty endured by the living. Consider the cash girls—young women working long hours for meager wages—who cannot scrape together even a nickel for the simple pleasure of a movie. While flowers bloom endlessly over a grave, these girls count their pennies, unable to afford the smallest of diversions from their exhausting daily grind.

This disparity extends further into the fabric of society, where desperation takes on different, more troubling forms. In saloons and taverns, women can be found drinking alongside men, or waiting patiently for their company, trading companionship for the jingling promise of silver dollars. It is not vice that draws them there, but necessity—the same hunger that drives so many choices among those who have nothing.

Perhaps most poignant is the story of a young woman earning just six dollars a week from selling goods behind some counter or storefront. The unrelenting hardship of her circumstances begins to erode something essential within her. Faced with such meager compensation for her labor, she grows reckless, increasingly indifferent to the judgments of God, the constraints of law, and the disapproval of public opinion. Her descent is not born of moral failing, but of a system that offers her so little that the rules governing polite society begin to seem irrelevant to her survival.

Together, these vignettes paint a portrait of a world deeply out of balance—one where extravagant sums are lavished upon the dead to preserve mere memory, while the living are left to navigate poverty, temptation, and desperation with next to nothing to sustain them.
outputs.L4:
# A Fortune for the Dead, A Pittance for the Living

In the heart of the city stands a mausoleum unlike any other—marble columns rising toward the sky, intricate carvings that speak of wealth beyond measure, and always, without fail, an abundance of fresh flowers cascading across its steps. This is the final resting place of a merchant whose name once commanded respect in every counting house and trading floor. His will, meticulous down to the last provision, decreed that $25,000 be spent annually—not on charity, not on the advancement of any cause, but on flowers. Roses, lilies, orchids flown in from distant countries—all so that his tomb would never want for beauty, so that his memory would be perpetually wreathed in fragrance and color, undimmed by time or neglect.

Year after year, gardeners tend to this arrangement with religious devotion. The flowers arrive fresh each week, are arranged with careful artistry, wilt, and are replaced—an endless cycle of expenditure that will continue long after anyone who knew the merchant in life has themselves passed into memory.

And yet, just blocks away from this monument to vanity, the living struggle to survive on wages that would make such extravagance seem obscene by comparison.

Consider the cash girls—those young women who spend their days running between counters and registers in the city's grand department stores, calves aching, fingers cramped, earning perhaps three or four dollars for an entire week's labor. They return home to cramped tenements, to meals that stretch thin, to lives measured out in exhausting increments of survival.

Consider too the women who frequent the saloons, not for revelry but for the cheap warmth of a stove, the flickering gaslight, a moment's respite from cold rooms and colder prospects. For some, it is the only accessible refuge from loneliness and destitution—a poor substitute for comfort, but comfort nonetheless in a world that offers them little else.

Consider the countless low-wage workers—seamstresses hunched over needlework until their eyes fail, laundresses with hands raw from lye and hot water, factory girls who trade their health for pennies—all laboring under conditions that would seem intolerable to those who never had to endure them, all struggling to afford bread, rent, medicine, the basic dignities of existence.

These women ask for so little: a living wage, safe conditions, perhaps a moment's respite from ceaseless toil. Yet society finds it easier to lavish $25,000 annually on flowers for a corpse than to ensure that a single living, breathing woman might eat properly or rest without fear.

This is the searing paradox at the heart of our economic order: that death can command such devotion, such expenditure, such careful attention to aesthetic perfection, while life—vibrant, struggling, desperate life—goes unnoticed and unaided. The merchant's flowers will bloom eternally, replenished by his fortune, while the women who might have benefited from even a fraction of that wealth wither in obscurity, their needs deemed less worthy of consideration than the appearance of a tomb.

It raises an uncomfortable question that society would rather leave unasked: What does it say about our values when we invest more thought, more money, more care into monuments for the dead than into the wellbeing of the living? When a man's vanity in death outweighs the desperate needs of women barely surviving in life? 

The flowers on that tomb are beautiful, no doubt—but their beauty is built upon a foundation of willful blindness, a testament not just to one man's wealth, but to a broader societal failure to recognize where true value ought to lie: not in marble and roses for the departed, but in bread and dignity for the living.
outputs.L5:
# The Tomb as Place

Every tomb is, above all, a place—a fixed point in the landscape where memory settles and time seems to pause. Unlike other structures built for the living, a tomb serves the dead, yet paradoxically it exists entirely for those who remain. It is a place of visitation, contemplation, and remembrance, where the boundary between past and present grows thin.

The significance of *the* tomb—any particular tomb—lies not merely in its architecture or the remains it holds, but in what it represents to those who seek it out. A tomb transforms an ordinary location into something sacred. The pyramids of Giza, the Taj Mahal, the humble grave in a village churchyard—each demonstrates how death, when marked and honored, creates place out of mere space.

Throughout history, civilizations have invested extraordinary effort into tomb-building precisely because the *place* of burial matters. Ancient Egyptians believed the tomb was a threshold to eternity, meticulously prepared for the soul's journey. Medieval Europeans built elaborate mausoleums to secure both earthly memory and heavenly favor. Even simple burial mounds speak to a universal human need: to mark a place as meaningful, to say "someone was here, someone mattered."

What makes a tomb different from other places is this duality—it belongs simultaneously to the dead and the living. The dead cannot experience the place; the living cannot fully possess it, since it belongs to memory and reverence rather than daily use. This tension gives tombs their particular power. Visitors to a tomb often report feelings of solemnity, connection, or quiet reflection, sensations tied directly to the *placeness* of the site—its physical presence, its history, its silent testimony.

In this way, the tomb stands as one of humanity's oldest architectural achievements: not a building for living, but a place for remembering—where stone and earth hold the weight of a life once lived, and where "the place" becomes inseparable from the story it protects.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Carl Sandburg-style free verse poem contrasting a millionaire's lavish tomb with the struggles of poor working women in the city.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Tomb and the Laundry

They put up a stone for him, a big gray stone
with angels cut into the corners and his name
spelled out in letters a foot high,
GARRISON, and under it the dates,
and under the dates nothing—
just Indiana limestone and forty tons of silence.

He made his money in wheat and freight cars,
in the small print of contracts,
in the spaces between what men are paid
and what men make for others.
Forty years he squeezed the city
like a fist around a sponge,
and this is what came out at the end:
a granite house for his bones,
bigger than any room
the women ever slept in
who washed his shirts.

*

Down on Halsted Street the laundries steam all night.
The women go in at six and come out at six,
gray-faced, hands boiled red,
carrying the smell of somebody else's dirt
home to their own kitchens
where the coffee is thin
and the children are already asleep
because waiting up costs money too—
money for coal, money for light.

Mrs. Kaminski presses shirts for nine hours a day.
Her thumb has a permanent white scar
where the iron kissed her two winters back.
She will not have a stone.
She will have a wooden marker, maybe,
if her son remembers, if the ground isn't too dear,
in the cheap part of the cemetery
where the grass grows over everybody the same,
sudden and green and indifferent,
the way grass doesn't care whose bones it's feeding on.

*

I have seen the tomb of Garrison.
The bronze door alone cost more
than Mrs. Kaminski will earn
in the years she has left to her,
however many those turn out to be,
counted out in irons lifted, shirts folded,
sheets carried up four flights of stairs.

Death, they say, is the great leveler.
I say death is a landlord too,
and some get the penthouse
and some get the alley,
and the moon doesn't care,
shining down on the limestone angels
the same as it shines
on the tar-paper roofs
where the wash hangs out to dry,
white shirts moving in the wind
like small surrendering flags.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a socially critical poem in the Chicago Poems tradition, juxtaposing extravagant funeral upkeep with urban poverty and vice.
counterfactuals.output:
# Marble and Ash

They spent forty thousand dollars on the mausoleum,
White marble hauled in on flatbed trucks,
Angels with their wings spread wide as charity,
And nobody living in that family
Has slept in a house with heat all winter.

I know a woman on Halsted Street
Who feeds her children bread and coffee,
Bread and coffee, bread and coffee,
Six days running, and on the seventh
She stands in line at the mission
With her hat in her hand like a beggar's cup.

Down at the cemetery the grass is trimmed
By men who get paid to make death look prosperous,
Green as money, green as the ten-dollar bills
That never make it to Halsted Street,
Never make it past the men in silk vests
Who count losses at the track and call it business.

I have seen the dead ride finer
Than the living ever rode,
Hearses black and polished like piano keys,
Horses draped in velvet, stepping slow,
While the woman's children walk to school
In shoes with cardboard for soles.

There is a saloon on the corner
Where the men go to forget
What the marble reminds them of—
That somewhere uptown a man they'll never meet
Is buried with more comfort
Than they've known in all their working lives.

The gravestone says BELOVED FATHER,
Carved deep so the rain won't wash it out.
Down the block a father sleeps in a doorway,
No stone, no name, no marble angel,
Just the cold and the going on,
The go on, the go on, the terrible go on
Of the living, who inherit nothing
But the bill for keeping the dead so well.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a poem about class inequality — a dead millionaire's endless flower budget versus working girls scraping by on six dollars a week.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ledger

They laid him out in a box lined with silk,
a hundred thousand dollars of hothouse bloom
piled high enough to drown the sight of him—
roses flown in off-season, lilies bred
for whiteness, nothing left to chance or God.
The papers called it *fitting tribute*, called it
*a life well celebrated*. Called it nothing
like what it was: a receipt.

Meanwhile,
some girl is counting nickels on a counter,
six dollars for the week and rent is four,
and the shoes she's wearing have a paper heart
tucked into the sole to hide the hole.
She sells the very flowers piled on his casket,
her fingers cut on wire and green tape,
a nickel a dozen for the arranging,
a nickel more if the boss don't feel like shorting her.

No one sends *her* lilies. No one flies
a hothouse rose across three states to mark
the small catastrophe of her one life—
the missed meals, the mended stockings, the room
she shares with two other girls and a leaking sink.
She will not get a box lined with silk.
She'll get a number on a county form,
a plot of ground no wider than her cot,
and maybe, if her sister has the coin,
a single flower, already halfway dead,
bought cheap because it's Tuesday and it's wilting—
the same flower, perhaps, grown in same dirt
as those that drowned a rich man in his sleep.

Funny, how the earth don't know the difference.
Grows the rose the same for him as her.
It's only after, in the counting house
of grief, someone decides whose flowers cost
a hundred thousand, and whose flowers don't cost
anything at all, being a girl's own hands
holding the cheap bouquet she can't afford
over the dirt already closing in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose free verse in the style of early 20th-century American realism poets, depicting a wealthy man's tomb alongside images of the urban poor at night.
counterfactuals.output:
**Marble for the Dead**

They cut him a house of granite
on the hill above the cemetery gates,
with iron doors that lock from the outside
and an angel kneeling, wings folded,
carved by Italian hands for eleven thousand dollars.
His name is chiseled deep enough to outlast
three generations of weather.
BELOVED, it says. FATHER. PILLAR OF THE CITY.

Down in the flats along the river
the poor are also lying down for the night,
under newspapers instead of granite,
in doorways instead of eleven thousand dollars.
No one carves their names in anything.
The wind writes them in ash on the sidewalk
and by morning they are gone.

A woman sells the last of her violets
under a gas lamp that gutters like a held breath.
A boy sleeps standing up against a warehouse wall,
his stomach a fist, his coat a rumor of a coat.
Somewhere a baby is crying the way babies cry
when there is no more milk in the house—
not loud, just steady, like a leak in a pipe
nobody has money to fix.

The dead man does not hear them.
He is done with hearing.
His tomb has a lock and a key
kept by a groundskeeper who also sleeps hungry,
who also has children coughing in a cold room,
who tends the marble every morning
because that is the job, and the job is money,
and money is what separates
a house that lasts forever
from a doorway that lasts until dawn.

The stars come out over both of them equally.
That is the only democracy this city has left—
the sky, indifferent, huge, unlocked,
falling the same cold light
on granite angels
and on the boy who has no name
carved anywhere,
who will not be remembered,
who is, tonight, still breathing,
which is more than the rich man can say,
lying there
in his eleven-thousand-dollar silence,
his name growing fainter
with every American rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
